Statement II: 3 + 4 = 7 makes B lie on segment AC, so the points are collinear and no circle passes through all three — answer NO. Each statement alone determines a definite answer, so B. (Noted defect: the two statements describe mutually inconsistent configurations for the same points, but each is independently sufficient.) The two Statements describe MUTUALLY INCONSISTENT configurations for the same three points (I gives a valid triangle, II gives collinear points), so the item cannot be internally consistent. Each is independently sufficient, so (b) stands either way.

For consecutive odd integers x + y = 4(k + 1), a multiple of 4. Statement I gives (x+y)^4 = 256 so x + y = 4 or -4 (from (1,3) and (-3,-1)) — not unique. Statement II gives x + y in {0, -4, -8, ...} — not unique. Together only x + y = -4 survives (4^3 = 64 is not < 16), confirmed by enumeration. RUNNER-UP: option B, if 'Can the value be determined uniquely?' is read strictly self-referentially as a yes/no question, since each statement alone answers 'no, not uniquely'; that reading makes Statement II's construction pointless, so C is the design intent. ADJUDICATED BY HAND -- the two blind passes DISAGREED here (B vs C). Both computed the same facts: consecutive odd integers force \(x+y\) to be a multiple of 4; Statement I gives \(x+y=\pm 4\) and Statement II gives \(x+y \in \{0,-4,-8,\dots\}\), neither unique, while together only \(-4\) survives. They differed on whether a definite 'no, not uniquely' itself counts as ANSWERING the printed yes/no Question, which would give (b). That reading is rejected on two grounds: it makes the answer independent of what Statement II says, so the setter's second statement would serve no purpose; and it would make option (d) unreachable for any 'can X be determined' item, yet (d) is offered and is the answer to three other items in this same block. This is a reading of data-sufficiency convention, not a computation, and the alternative is defensible.

Enumeration over p, q in 1..6 gives both parities under each statement, and together they carry the same single fact, so still insufficient.
